title: Where Are You? — Serpent, Fruit, Garment
blocks: Brothers and sisters, in the last two lessons we read a very beautiful beginning: God speaks and chaos gives way; God bends down and settles the man in a garden. Chapter 1 says "good" seven times; chapter 2 says "not good" once, and God himself supplies what was missing. And as chapter 2 closes, the text says, "The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed."

The question this lesson puts to us is the most fundamental question in the whole Bible: why is it that when a person knows he has done wrong, his first reaction is not to own it but to hide? Why is it that after a husband and wife quarrel, the first thing out of anyone's mouth is not an apology but "this is your fault"?

Let me give you the answer up front: the root of sin is not that piece of fruit. It is wanting to define good and evil for yourself, wanting to sit in God's chair. And the first thing God says after the man hides is not a verdict. It is a search.
1. The Distance of a Single Vowel
Verse 1: "Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made."

Brothers and sisters, there is a detail here that no translation can carry across. The last verse of chapter 2 says the man and his wife were "naked", in Hebrew עֲרוּמִּים (*arumim*); the first verse of chapter 3 says the serpent was "subtle", in Hebrew עָרוּם (*arum*). The two words are nearly identical — a whisker apart. The author has done this on purpose. In the instant you turn the page, he wants you to hear an uneasy echo: that unashamed nakedness is about to meet something very shrewd.

And what does the text tell us about this serpent? Only that it is one of the creatures "which Yahweh God had made." No name, no origin, no backstory. Revelation 12:9 will later tell us that the old serpent is the devil, Satan — but Genesis 3 deliberately declines to introduce him.

Why? Because he is not the protagonist of this chapter. Brothers and sisters, Satan's favourite sermon is a sermon about Satan. The text writes him extremely small: a creature, two questions, and then he leaves the stage and is never mentioned again in the chapter. If you find yourself talking about the enemy more warmly than you talk about Christ, this verse is asking you to turn the camera back.
If God knew they would eat, why did he put that tree in the middle of the garden at all?

Because without that tree there could be no real love. Love presupposes the freedom not to love; obedience presupposes the freedom not to obey. A creature that cannot say no is a machine, not a person capable of loving God back. God did not lay a trap: he stated the boundary plainly and stated the consequence in advance — that is responsible dealing, not baiting a hook. And notice that the tree was not hidden. It stood "in the middle of the garden", in plain sight every day; the freedom God gave was "you may freely eat of every tree of the garden", with exactly one prohibition. So the problem was never that God was stingy. It is that in a place of overwhelming generosity, human beings kept staring at the single boundary.
2. The Three Moves of Temptation: Twist, Trim, Deny
What comes next is the most important anatomy lesson on temptation in the whole Bible. The serpent speaks only twice, and in those two speeches he completes three moves.

The first move is to twist. He says, "Has God really said, 'You shall not eat of any tree of the garden'?" What God actually said was, "You may freely eat of every tree of the garden; but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil." The serpent turns "all of them, except one" into "none of them." The word מִכֹּל (*mikol*, "every / any") has simply been shifted. Brothers and sisters, he does not begin by attacking God's existence. He begins by attacking God's generosity.

The second move is to trim — and this time it is the human being who does it. The woman answers, "We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, 'You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.'" Compare three points. She drops "freely" — God said they might eat *freely*. She adds "you shall not touch it" — God never said that. And she softens "you will surely die" into "lest you die" — the emphatic Hebrew construction is gone, and a flat statement has become a possibility.

Brothers and sisters, notice that these two distortions happen at the same time: the grace God spoke is shrunk, and the prohibition God spoke is inflated. That is exactly the recipe of legalism — make God sound a little stingier, then add extra rules of your own and imagine it is safer that way. And the result? The one who added the rules is the first to fall.

The third move is to deny. The serpent says, "You won't really die." In Hebrew that is לֹא־מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן (*lo-mot temutun*). He uses exactly the same emphatic construction God used, and simply puts a "not" in front of it. This is the first outright lie in the Bible, and its method is not to invent a rival account. It is to take God's own words untouched and hang a negative on the front.

And then he offers the real bait: "you will be like God, knowing good and evil." כֵּאלֹהִים (*ke'Elohim*), like God. Brothers and sisters, this is the heart of it. The root of humanity's fall is not wanting that fruit. It is wanting that chair.
The serpent said, "You won't really die" — but Adam lived over nine hundred years afterwards. Was the serpent right?

The Hebrew of Genesis 2:17 is "in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die" (מוֹת תָּמוּת), literally "dying, you shall die" — it speaks of the moment death enters, not the moment breathing stops. And that moment did happen: they hid, and the relationship was cut; they were driven from the garden, away from the tree of life; and then chapter 5 tolls "and he died" eight times over. Death in Scripture is at its core separation from God, and physical death is the consequence of that. So the most insidious thing about the serpent's line is not that it is entirely false but that it is half true — it takes "you will not drop dead immediately" and sells it as "nothing will happen." A great many temptations still work that way today: they do not deny the consequence, they only make the consequence feel far away.
When Eve answered the serpent she added "you shall not touch it." Did she add that herself? Does it matter?

What God said in Genesis 2:17 was "you shall not eat"; he never said "you shall not touch." Eve's answer simultaneously adds something ("you shall not touch it"), subtracts something (God said "you may *freely* eat of every tree"; she says "we may eat fruit from the trees of the garden", with "freely" removed), and weakens the force (God said "you will surely die"; she says "lest you die"). It matters a great deal, because it shows that the first step of temptation is not to make a person sin — it is to get God's word moved slightly. Rules added on make God feel harsh; grace trimmed away makes God feel stingy; and once the force is softened, a boundary stops being a boundary. So guarding God's word means neither saying more on his behalf nor saying less.
3. A Light from the Original: "Knowing" Is Not Understanding — It Is Deciding
The phrase "knowing good and evil" has to be got right, or the whole chapter will be read crookedly.

"To know" is יָדַע (*yada*). In Hebrew this word is never merely an acquaintance with information — Genesis 4:1, "the man knew Eve his wife", uses this very verb. So יָדַע means deep involvement, first-hand experience, taking something to oneself.

And in Old Testament usage, "to know good and evil" often means having the competence to determine right and wrong for oneself. 2 Samuel 14:17 says the king is able "to discern good and evil", using this same pairing. So what the serpent promises is not "you will become better informed." It is "you will get to decide."

Brothers and sisters, this is precisely what 321 means by pride: leaving our originally intended position as human beings, seizing the rights that belong to God, wanting to stand in for God. What that tree forbade was never knowledge — God is not afraid of you being clever; he commands you to love him with all your mind. What that tree forbade was sitting down in the chair that defines good and evil.

Then verse 6 says, "When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise …" Look at that verb — "saw", וַתֵּרֶא (*vatere*). In chapter 1, "God saw that it was good" occurs seven times, from the same root. A dozen times over it has been God looking and God pronouncing good; here, for the first time, it becomes a human being looking and a human being pronouncing good.

And 1 John 2:16 says, "For all that is in the world — the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life — isn't the Father's, but is the world's." Brothers and sisters, those three phrases are copied straight out of Genesis 3:6: good for food is the lust of the flesh, a delight to the eyes is the lust of the eyes, and desirable to make one wise is the pride of life. Four thousand years, and the packaging has changed a thousand times; the formula has not changed once.

There is one more phrase that is easy to read past. Verse 6 says she "gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too", and the Hebrew has a preposition in front of "her husband" meaning "who was with her." Adam was not somewhere else. He was standing right there. He heard that entire conversation from beginning to end, and he did not say a word.
"Knowing good and evil" sounds like a good thing. Why did eating it cause such trouble?

The problem is not the knowing; it is who holds the right to define. The Hebrew "know" (יָדַע) is experiential knowledge, and "good and evil" in the Old Testament is often a merism for "everything" — the way we say "the long and the short of it." So what that tree offered was the authority to decide for yourself what counts as good and what counts as bad. That is precisely the act of a creature stepping outside his originally intended position. When a person defines good and evil for himself, the result is not more freedom; it is that every relationship has to be renegotiated — who is right, who is wrong, who owes whom. The blame-shifting, the covering up and the mutual accusation that follow in chapter 3 are the inevitable consequence of that authority changing hands.
4. Where Are You — the First Question in the Whole Bible

Verse 7 says their eyes were opened. The serpent was right; their eyes did open. And what did they see once they were open? "They both knew that they were naked." The same body, the same marriage, the same garden — swap out one pair of eyes and all that is left to see is shame.
Their first invention is a covering: they sew fig leaves together. And that garment, חֲגֹרֹת (*chagorot*), is only a loincloth — it covers one part of a person, not the person.

Then verse 8: "They heard Yahweh God's voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day." That word "walking" is מִתְהַלֵּךְ (*mithalech*), a reflexive form with a habitual flavour — this is how he had always come and gone. Brothers and sisters, this was not the first time. God had been coming all along. What changed was not God's footsteps but the human response: the man and his wife "hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden."

And notice what they were hiding from — not the punishment, but the *presence*, מִפְּנֵי (*mipnei*), that face. The most immediate effect of sin is that a person no longer dares to look at the face he used to see every day.
Then comes verse 9, the first question in the whole Bible: "Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, 'Where are you?'" אַיֶּכָּה (*ayekah*).

Brothers and sisters, hold three things. First, this is the Bible's first question, and it is God who asks it. Second, God of course knows where Adam is; he asks so that Adam will say where he is. And third, most important of all: the one hiding is the man, and the one walking towards him is God. From its very first page, Christianity is not a religion of people searching for God. It is the good news of God searching for people.

Adam's answer is very honest and very dishonest at once: "I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself." He admits the behaviour and does not admit the reason. And "afraid", וָאִירָא (*va'ira*), is the first appearance of fear in the Bible — before sin came in, human beings did not know what fear was.

And then comes the classic deflection: "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it." One sentence, two deflections: first onto the woman, and then onto the One who gave him the woman. And the woman says, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate." Brothers and sisters, this is the moment relationships split open — with God, with each other, and within themselves, all at once.
"Where are you" — did God really not know where Adam was hiding?

Of course he knew. This is a pastoral question, not an investigative one. The first question in the whole Bible is not "what have you done?" but "where are you?" — God asks about the relationship before he asks about the case. And notice the order: God walked over first and then spoke; he was walking in the garden in the cool of the day, moving towards two people who were hiding. That verse runs all the way down to Luke 15, where the father runs towards the prodigal. So after someone falls, the most God-like thing you can do is not to interrogate the details first, but to walk over and ask, "Where are you right now?" Of course, what needs dealing with still gets dealt with afterwards — God went on to ask, "Who told you that you were naked?"
Why did God make them garments of skin instead of simply forgiving them?

Because covering costs something. What they made for themselves was fig leaves — the fastest thing to hand, costing nothing, and destined to wither. What God made was skins, which means an animal died. This is the first time blood is shed in the Bible because of human sin. From here the line runs straight through the Passover lamb, through the altar of Leviticus, to John the Baptist pointing at Jesus and saying, "Behold, the Lamb of God." So "just forgive and be done with it" sounds kind, but it treats sin far too lightly: real forgiveness has never meant that the account is ignored. It means someone else settled it for you. And the covering God gave was not so that they could keep hiding; it was so that they could stand in his presence.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "Where are you?" as God calling someone to account. This is the most common misreading from Chinese pulpits. The tone of the original is searching, not interrogation — it is how a shepherd asks. Preach it as a demand and the congregation's first impression of God becomes fear rather than grace. The test is simple: when the congregation has heard you, do they want to come back to God, or do they want to hide further?

The second is putting the whole blame on Eve. The text says plainly that she gave to "her husband with her, and he ate it, too" — Adam was standing right there, silent throughout. And Romans 5:12 lays sin at Adam's door, not Eve's. Preaching this chapter as "it was all the woman's fault" is unfaithful to the text, and it makes the women in the room carry for a lifetime a burden that was never theirs.

The third is preaching Genesis 3:16 as the standard model for marriage. "Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you" is a consequence of the fall — a diagnosis, not a prescription. And the next time that word "desire" appears is Genesis 4:7 — "sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you" — where it plainly means the wish to master. To take a curse and turn it into house rules is to enthrone brokenness as the standard.

The fourth is preaching the serpent as the lead in a horror film. The point of this chapter is how a human being leaves his originally intended position, not how formidable the devil is. Put the spotlight on the serpent and your congregation will walk out more afraid of the powers of darkness rather than more attentive to their own hearts.

The fifth, and the most important: preaching the curse and never reaching the garments of skin. Verse 21 says, "Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them." That is the summit of grace in the chapter. If the last image in your sermon is a closed gate, you have left out the last thing God did.
If a curse arrives the moment sin comes in, does that not make the promise in verse 15 rather less significant?

Quite the opposite — it is the most significant sentence in the chapter. Verse 15, "He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel", has been called by interpreters down the centuries the *protevangelium*, the first gospel. Notice two things. First, it is spoken to the serpent, not to the humans — the announcement of salvation is issued inside the judgement. Second, the text says "her offspring", and the Hebrew pronoun that follows is masculine singular, pointing to one person. So while human beings have not yet repented and are still deflecting blame onto each other, God has already spoken the way out. That is intensely practical for us: God does not start looking for a solution the moment you confess. His solution was ready before you fell.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: when something goes wrong in a Chinese family, the first instinct is often that family shame must not be aired in public, so the matter gets covered over. What has that to do with chapter 3? Brothers and sisters, everything. The first thing human beings did after sinning was sew leaves; the second was hide in the trees. Covering and hiding are the two most primitive movements of sin — and our culture has dressed them up as virtues. But look carefully: fig leaves wither, and God did not expose them either. God walked over and asked, "Where are you?" So the right direction is neither exposure nor concealment. It is that somebody is willing to speak first and walk towards the place where the other is hiding. If a church cannot be a place where saying it out loud does not get you discarded, then brothers and sisters will go on sewing leaves forever.

The second question: my elders often say human nature is basically good, while the Bible says people are born with a sinful nature — how do I hold those two together in conversation? My advice is not to open by contradicting them. When Mencius taught the goodness of human nature, what he saw was real: there genuinely is a longing for the good in the human heart, and a reluctance to see others suffer. Romans 2:15 says the Gentiles "show the work of the law written in their hearts" — Scripture grants this. The disagreement is not over whether people have an inclination towards good; it is over whether people can get back to God under their own power. So you might say it this way: you are right, there really is a strength towards the good inside a person; what I later discovered is that the strength cannot save me — I know what is right and I still cannot do it. And that is exactly what Romans 7 is about. Put like this, you do not deny what they have observed; you simply push the question one layer deeper.
7. Living 321 Out — Peace Comes from Returning to Your Own Place
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Adam was tempted in a garden of abundance and failed; the Lord Jesus was tempted in a barren wilderness and prevailed. Both were tempted; one said "this fruit is desirable", the other said "it is written." My example is very concrete: when temptation comes, go back to what God has said, not back to what I feel.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter tells us that the first move of temptation is to tamper with God's word: add a line, drop a line, soften the tone. So "the Bible is my standard" cannot stay a slogan; it requires that you actually know what God said. A person whose impression of God's word is vague will find it very hard to spot the version with one word changed.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — verse 8 speaks of "the cool of the day", and the Hebrew behind "cool" is רוּחַ (*ruach*), which is also the word for Spirit — the same word as the Spirit hovering over the waters in 1:2. God came, and the human beings hid. The Holy Spirit still comes today, and he comes for the same reason he came that day: not to catch you, but to find you.

Let Jesus be King — "you will be like God" is the manifesto of the old self. Letting Jesus be King is that sentence turned around: I am not God, I do not have to know everything, and I do not have to decide everything. Brothers and sisters, only when a person hands over the authority to define good and evil does he find peace. The thing you have been turning over and over and refusing to let go of is usually the very thing where you are still sitting in that chair.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — notice verse 15: "he will bruise your head" is said to the serpent, not to the human beings. While they were still awaiting sentence, God had already announced the enemy's end in the enemy's hearing. Your salvation is not something you negotiated. It was announced while you still had nothing to say. The glory can only go to him.

Establish God's system — Genesis 3:15 is the first war dispatch of God's kingdom. From that verse the whole Bible runs along one line, all the way to Golgotha, to an empty tomb, to Revelation 20. So establishing God's system is not starting from zero in a battle whose outcome is undecided; it is working along a line where victory has already been declared.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We are quite used to diagnosing people with "self-centred" and "selfless", and it is a useful instrument — but real people are never that tidy. The same person can be proud and ashamed at the same time; a controlling husband may have fear underneath; a sister who submits until she has almost disappeared may be acting out of injury. So this framework is a diagnostic aid, not a complete portrait of a human being. Never say to anyone, "You are the proud type." Using the instrument to file other people away is itself a form of self-centredness.
"Returning to our originally intended position" sounds passive. Is it telling people not to be ambitious?

No. Returning to our originally intended position is not doing nothing; it is not doing God's work. A human being's originally intended position includes governing, keeping, being fruitful and developing — that is an enormous field, not a small one. Only one thing is off limits: defining for God what is good and what is evil. So healthy ambition says, "I will give everything I have in the place God has given me"; unhealthy ambition says, "I will decide whether this is right or wrong." The practical test is simple: when your plan collides with God's word, which one do you change? A person who changes the plan is an ambitious servant. A person who changes the word has already taken the seat under that tree.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Question: "Where Are You?"
Brothers and sisters, the same question — "Where are you?" — sounds completely different falling into four different hearts.

The proud heart hears: "He must be asking somebody else." This heart reads chapter 3 with its eyes on Eve, on the serpent, on other people's weakness, and finishes the chapter without a scratch. 1 Corinthians 10:12 says, "Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn't fall." The place where Adam fell was the best set of conditions the world has ever offered. A good environment does not keep anybody standing.

The fearful heart hears: "He has come to get me." This heart begins composing its explanation the moment it hears God's voice. Brothers and sisters, read that verse carefully — God *called* to the man, וַיִּקְרָא (*vayiqra*), the same verb used in chapter 2 when the man named the animals. That is calling by name. John 10:3 says the shepherd "calls his own sheep by name." He is saying your name; he is not coming to arrest you.

The ashamed heart hears: "I cannot go out and face him looking like this." This heart is not unbelieving; it simply feels unworthy. Brothers and sisters, look at verse 21: God did not wait until they were clean before drawing near — God himself made the clothes and put them on. What people sew is leaves, and leaves wither; what God made was skin, and that required blood. You do not have to tidy yourself up first. He has already prepared the garment.

The wounded heart hears: "Here comes the reckoning again." This heart may genuinely have been condemned with a Bible in someone's hand, told to its face, "See — this is what disobedience gets you." Brothers and sisters, count the order of this chapter: God asks "Where are you?" first, then pronounces sentence; and after the sentence, he makes the clothes with his own hands. His order is: seek, explain, cover. What wounded you was not this chapter. It was the person who used this chapter as a stick.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, identify the fig leaf you are currently sewing. It might be a story you tell, an image you maintain, a kind of busyness, or the words "I'm fine." Write it down, and then say to God in prayer, "Lord, I sewed this myself, and I know it will wither."

Second, practise apologising without "but". If you get something wrong this week, say plainly, "I was wrong" — full stop. No "but he also …", no "I was only …". Adam's failure was not in the eating; it was in what he said after the eating.

Third, change one altered sentence back. Think about whether there is a sentence about God inside you that has quietly been tampered with — something like "God probably will not bother with me", or "God only likes people who perform well." Find a verse, change it back, and write it somewhere you will see it.

Fourth, walk towards someone who is still hiding. This week, find one person you know is struggling and whom nobody has asked, and say, "How have you been lately?" You do not have to give advice. Just take one step in the direction of where he is hiding.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences: the first question in the Bible is asked by God, and it is "Where are you?" — the human being hid and God spoke first to look for him; the first instinct after doing wrong is to cover up and shift blame, and that is not a flaw in your personality, it is humanity's oldest habit; and the story does not end with people being driven out — it ends with God making them clothes with his own hands.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer sit in the seat that defines good and evil; I am not God, and I do not have to know everything.
I declare that I will hold God's word exactly as it stands, adding nothing to it and taking nothing from it.
I declare that when I hear him call my name, I will answer, and not hide among the trees again.
I declare that what covers me is not the leaves I sewed, but the garment he made with his own hands.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be verse 21.

Read the chapter through and you watch a sequence of movements all running downhill: doubt, reaching out, eating, eyes opening, sewing leaves, hiding, deflecting, being cursed, being driven out. It is one long descending line.
And then, just before they are driven out, the text inserts a sentence: "Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them."

Weigh that picture. To have skin, something must first die. In that garden, on that day, a life was taken so that two people in hiding would have something to wear. What they made covered the waist; what God made covered them from shoulder to foot.

And thousands of years later Galatians 3:27 says, "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Brothers and sisters, the same action. God is still preparing garments for people in hiding — only this time the one who was taken has a name.

So chapter 3 is not a chapter about failure. It is the first place in the Bible where the gospel is preached. Verse 15 declares victory in the hearing of the enemy; verse 21 puts grace onto human beings in the form of a coat. Your failure is real — and so is the fact that God walked into the garden.

The focus is not on how hard I fell, not on how long I have been hiding, and not on how much I still have unresolved. The focus is on Jesus — he is the offspring of the woman, and he is the Lamb whose skin was taken so that I would have something to wear. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to stop sewing leaves, and when we hear him call our name, to walk out from among the trees. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear conviction.
1. ★★ The serpent's three moves are twist, trim and deny. Give one example of each that you have actually heard online or among people this week.
2. ★★★ The problem with "knowing good and evil" is not the knowing but who has the right to define. How would you put that in your own words to someone new?
3. ★ God's first question is "Where are you?", not "What have you done?" What does that order tell us about the kind of God he is?
4. ★★ People covered themselves with fig leaves; God covered them with skins. What is the difference between those two coverings, and why does the difference matter?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, saying and walking, to digest the idea until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can judge this for myself), fearful (afraid of being seen as I am), ashamed (I cannot be seen like this), wounded (someone once used the truth to humiliate me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, 'Where are you?'" Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?

7. ★★ Is there something you are currently covering with a "leaf" — something nobody knows and you would rather not discuss? You do not have to say what it is. Only say this: who is it that you are afraid will find out?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "This lesson showed me the thing I am most likely to appoint myself judge over is …"
9. ★★ This week, in which matter will you hand the right of definition back to God — that is, do what Scripture says even though you disagree? Name it.

Leader's reminder: questions five and seven will touch shame. If someone weeps or falls silent, stop the discussion and stay with him; do not press for details, and never require anyone to confess publicly. If long-standing guilt or trauma is involved, follow up privately afterwards and help him find pastoral or professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ "Where are you?" asks about the relationship before the case. Which conversation in your home this week should begin with the relationship? Say who, and say the sentence you will use.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, is there someone whose faults you keep pursuing without ever asking how he is?
